{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nv-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"ed2ca0fdb34ce9a242194cbd0e00e1711a88a12d144e0ccca66f75c124bec78b","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nv-class-c:lineage:32","source_registry_sha256":"3e184808e042e052d0c78d0dff47c50b34a56560f428649c492afe10bc7ba712","source_liveness_sha256":"0dfbf3aa4b4798b88d69252e076642b5f0a38751c5010711fbce93c8a7d6e292"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Special driving conditions: night, bad weather, emergencies, flash floods, work zones and stopped emergency vehicles","heading":"C — Special driving conditions: night driving and headlights, bad weather and winter tires, skids, vehicle emergencies, running off the road, blowouts, flash floods, work zones and stopped emergency vehicles","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Special driving conditions: night driving and headlights, bad weather and winter tires, skids, vehicle emergencies, running off the road, blowouts, flash floods, work zones and stopped emergency vehicles
Knowledge domain: how to adjust for darkness and bad weather, when headlights and high beams are required, what to do when brakes, the gas pedal, steering, wipers, headlights or a tire fail, how to recover from running off the pavement, why flooded roads must be avoided, how to drive through work zones, and the duty to slow and move over for stopped emergency and service vehicles.

FACT_ID: sec08-F01 | anchor: A01
Night driving is always harder and more hazardous than daytime driving because you see less, later and not as far, and oncoming headlight glare adds to the difficulty. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F02 | anchor: A01
At night, always be able to stop within the distance your headlights light up, and keep your speed under control and within posted limits. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F03 | anchor: A01
Do not look straight into oncoming headlights; look down toward the right side of your lane, using the edge line or center line as a guide. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F04 | anchor: A01
Never wear sunglasses when driving at night, and keep the windshield clean inside and out. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F05 | anchor: A01
Headlights are required by law from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, whenever there is not enough light, and whenever people or vehicles cannot be seen clearly at 1,000 feet. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F06 | anchor: A01
Headlights are also required when an official traffic control device directs you to use them, and using them in rain, snow or fog is advisable. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F07 | anchor: A01
Use high beams in open country at night, but switch to low beams at least 500 feet before meeting an oncoming vehicle and 300 feet before reaching a vehicle you are following. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F08 | anchor: A01
Do not drive with only the parking lights on; you may flash your headlights to warn a driver ahead that you plan to pass. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F09 | anchor: A02
The most important thing in bad weather is to slow down, since stopping distances on slippery roads can be 2 to 10 times longer than on dry pavement. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F10 | anchor: A02
For snowy or icy roads, fit chains, snow tires or all-weather radials, and remember that even well-equipped vehicles can slide. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F11 | anchor: A02
On snow or ice, start very slowly, test your brakes gently to learn how well you can stop, and begin slowing well before intersections and turns. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F12 | anchor: A02
No speed is completely safe on snow and ice, because conditions change with sun, shade and sanding from one block or stretch of road to the next. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F13 | anchor: A02
On slippery roads, gentle braking with a slow, light touch-and-release pattern helps you stop safely, but a vehicle with ABS needs firm, continuous pedal pressure for the anti-lock feature to work. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F14 | anchor: A02
Studded snow tires may be used only from October 1 through April 30; tires with retractable studs are legal all year, but the studs may be engaged only within those dates. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F15 | anchor: A02
Skidding means the tires have lost traction; it happens most on ice or packed snow but also on wet pavement or gravel. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec08-F16 | anchor: A03
If the brakes fail, pump the pedal; if they still do not respond, use the parking brake and shift to a lower gear if possible, but never shift into park. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-F17 | anchor: A03
After driving through deep water, test your brakes; dry them by driving slowly in low gear while braking lightly, testing about every 200 feet until they work normally. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-F18 | anchor: A03
If the gas pedal sticks, quickly press it hard and release; if it stays stuck, shift to neutral, brake, and pull off to the right and stop, never shifting into park. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-F19 | anchor: A03
If you see smoke rising from the engine area, slow, get off the road and shut off the ignition immediately, and open the hood with extreme caution. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-F20 | anchor: A03
Never use water on a vehicle fire, because burning gasoline floats and spreads; use a chemical extinguisher or sand or dirt, and if the fire cannot be stopped move at least 100 feet away. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-F21 | anchor: A03
If steering fails, ease off the accelerator; if the car holds its lane, slow and brake gently with flashers on, but brake hard if it heads off the road or toward a vehicle or pedestrian. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-F22 | anchor: A03
If a vehicle comes at you in your lane, slow down, sound the horn, flash your headlights and pull as far right as is safe, without swerving into the lane it left. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec08-F23 | anchor: A04
Running off the road causes serious single-vehicle crashes that account for many Nevada deaths, with fatigue, inattention and speeding as major factors. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F24 | anchor: A04
If you drift onto the shoulder, stay calm, lift off the gas, brake only carefully, grip the wheel firmly, and do not swerve back; stay on the shoulder until fully in control, then ease back onto the road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F25 | anchor: A04
In a tire blowout, grip the wheel firmly and ease off the gas without hitting the brakes, then brake gently only once the vehicle is under control and has slowed. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F26 | anchor: A04
More than half of all flash flood deaths involve vehicles, and less than 1 inch of water can make a driver lose control. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F27 | anchor: A04
Most vehicles can float in 2 feet of water or less, and a car moving fast can be pushed off the road by only 6 inches of water. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F28 | anchor: A04
Never try to drive through a flooded road; turn around and take another route or wait for the water to go down, since its depth and whether the road beneath has washed out cannot be judged. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F29 | anchor: A04
If your vehicle stalls in rising flood water and it is safe, leave it at once and get to higher ground. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F30 | anchor: A05
The only sure flood safety rule is to turn around and stay off flooded roads, and you must never drive around barricades that officials have put up. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-F31 | anchor: A05
Work zones are marked with orange signs, cones and barrels; lanes narrow, surfaces are rough and traffic may stop completely, so stay alert and expect stopped cars ahead. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-F32 | anchor: A05
Moving barriers or signs to drive onto a closed road is illegal and carries double penalties for work-zone violations. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-F33 | anchor: A05
Speeding fines double in work zones; black and white speed limit signs are regulatory, while orange speed limit signs are advisory and suggest slower, safer speeds. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-F34 | anchor: A05
Whenever you see orange signs, slow down, watch for workers and equipment, follow flaggers' instructions and merge carefully and cooperatively. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-F35 | anchor: A06
When approaching a stopped emergency, utility or service vehicle such as a police car, tow truck, NDOT vehicle or garbage truck, slow to a reasonable speed below the posted limit, proceed with caution and be ready to stop (NRS 484B.607). [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-F36 | anchor: A06
When passing such a stopped vehicle, move if possible into a lane not next to the one it occupies, unless road, traffic or weather conditions make that unsafe or impossible. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-F37 | anchor: A06
The slow-down duty also applies when approaching a vehicle showing non-flashing blue lights in certain circumstances and when someone is repairing a vehicle. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-F38 | anchor: A06
Drivers of non-emergency vehicles may not stop on a highway shoulder marked for emergency use. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0061]

Misconceptions: low beams are not just for city streets, they are required before meeting or following another vehicle; sunglasses never help at night; pumping is not the method for an ABS car on ice, firm steady pressure is; a few inches of moving water is not safe to drive through; orange speed signs are advisory but black and white ones are the law; when a car runs onto the shoulder, swerving straight back is the mistake.
Mnemonics: five hundred to meet, three hundred to follow; half an hour after sunset, half an hour before sunrise; turn around, don't drown; never park when brakes or pedal fail; slow down and move over.
Glossary: low beams means the dipped headlight setting used near other vehicles; skid means the tires losing traction; blowout means a tire suddenly losing air; flash flood means sudden fast-rising water after storms or thaw; advisory speed means a suggested safer speed on an orange sign; move over means changing out of the lane next to a stopped emergency vehicle.
Dynamic facts: the studded-tire season dates, work-zone penalties and the shoulder-use list are set by law and can change by statute, so confirm them against the current Nevada handbook.
